title: Anti-Corruption Icon Anna Hazare Hospitalised in Mumbai With Viral Infection
excerpt: The veteran social activist was admitted to Bombay Hospital after severe dehydration and a viral infection, with doctors monitoring his condition closely.
body:
• Anna Hazare was admitted to Bombay Hospital in Mumbai on Monday after severe dehydration and a viral infection
  • Reports conflict on whether he was placed in the ICU or a regular ward; his treating physician said he is stable and under investigation
  • The veteran activist had initially been receiving treatment near his native village of Ralegan Siddhi before being transferred to Mumbai
  • Hazare, known for his anti-corruption movement that shaped India's Lokpal Act, has had multiple hospitalisations linked to his history of hunger strikes

Anna Hazare, the Gandhian social activist whose anti-corruption movement galvanised millions of Indians in 2011, was admitted to Bombay Hospital in Mumbai on Monday after his health deteriorated due to a severe viral infection and acute dehydration.

The veteran reformer had been receiving treatment at a medical facility near his native village of Ralegan Siddhi in Maharashtra when complications prompted his transfer to Mumbai for advanced care, according to multiple reports citing medical sources.

Conflicting Reports on ICU Admission

Initial reports from IANS and several outlets stated that Hazare was admitted to the intensive care unit under the care of Dr Gautam Bhansali. However, Dr Bhansali subsequently clarified to reporters that Hazare was admitted to a regular ward, not the ICU.

https://x.com/ndtv/status/2094588466428518540

"He is stable and under investigation. He has been admitted to a ward, not in the ICU," Dr Bhansali said. "He had come for a regular check-up. There is some viral infection. There is nothing related to kidneys."

Doctors said Hazare had experienced difficulty passing urine due to severe dehydration on arrival. His condition improved considerably after fluid administration. The medical team ruled out kidney-related complications, attributing the urinary difficulty solely to dehydration. Further diagnostic tests were scheduled for Tuesday to assess the extent of the viral infection.

A Pattern of Health Scares

The hospitalisation follows a familiar pattern for the activist, whose decades of hunger strikes and protest campaigns have taken a cumulative toll on his body. After his landmark 12-day fast at Ramlila Maidan in 2011, Hazare was hospitalised at Medanta in Gurugram with severe dehydration and exhaustion, having lost approximately 7.5 kilograms.

Subsequent hospital stays have followed fasts and agitations: viral fever and falling blood pressure during a 2011 Mumbai fast; an ICU setup in Ralegan Siddhi during a 2013 fast; hospitalisation in Ahmednagar in 2016; an ICU admission in 2019 after a seven-day hunger strike; and treatment at Ruby Hall Clinic in Pune in 2021 after chest pain and a coronary blockage.

"Democracy works through dialogue, not diktat. I have never used violence in any of my hunger strikes."

— Anna Hazare's recurring theme of nonviolent reform

Still Active at 87

Despite his age and health history, Hazare has remained active in public life. In June 2026, he warned of an indefinite hunger strike if the Maharashtra government did not withdraw new RTI rules he said favoured officials over citizens. After talks with the state Chief Information Commissioner, the government stayed the rules, though Hazare called the stay insufficient and demanded a full rollback.

In July, he joined a silent protest in support of students agitating over examination paper leaks and demanding the education minister's resignation. He left the venue after about an hour when he felt unwell. He subsequently wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi urging dialogue with the protesting students.

Why the Diaspora Watches

Hazare holds a singular place in modern Indian civic history. His "I Am Anna" movement in 2011 mobilised unprecedented public participation in the fight against corruption and ultimately contributed to the passage of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act in 2013. For millions in the Indian diaspora who participated in or watched the movement from abroad, his health remains a matter of personal concern.

He was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1992 for his work in transforming Ralegan Siddhi into a model village through watershed development, afforestation, and rural self-reliance. His later split with Arvind Kejriwal and the Aam Aadmi Party, which grew out of the same movement, marked a divergence between his vision of civic activism and electoral politics.

What's Next

An official medical update is expected after diagnostic evaluations are completed on Tuesday. Supporters and political figures across party lines have expressed concern and wished him a speedy recovery. For now, the facts remain straightforward: the activist who spent decades asking the country to stand with him is under close medical observation in a Mumbai hospital, and the viral infection and dehydration that brought him there are being treated.
